items.prompt:
(1) Which observation best distinguishes chemical change from a change of state?
A. The shape changes
B. Bubbles appear
C. A new substance forms
D. The sample becomes warmer [1]

(2) Which description explains an endothermic reaction?
A. It absorbs energy from surroundings
B. It releases energy to surroundings
C. It has no energy change
D. It requires no starting energy [1]

(3) What heat is gained by 50 g water warming by 4 °C, with c=4.2 J/(g °C) and q=mcΔT?
A. 840 J
B. 52.5 J
C. 0.84 J
D. 210 J [1]

(4) Why can a burning fuel warm a pan?
A. Breaking fuel bonds is the heat-releasing step
B. The pan heats because fuel absorbs energy
C. Combustion transfers energy to the pan
D. Heat release requires the pan to react [1]

(5) Which comparison of wind generation with fuel combustion is sound?
A. No operating combustion; weather-dependent output
B. Low operating emissions; weather-independent output
C. No fuel combustion; no construction impacts
D. Variable weather dependence; no energy transfer [1]

(6) What does a steeper gradient on a gas-volume against time curve mean?
A. A larger final gas volume
B. A slower gas-production rate
C. A smaller final gas volume
D. A higher gas-production rate [1]

(7) Why can higher solution concentration increase rate at constant temperature?
A. Average particle kinetic energy increases
B. The activation-energy barrier becomes lower
C. Collisions transfer greater energy individually
D. Successful collisions occur more frequently [1]

(8) How does a suitable catalyst increase reaction rate?
A. By increasing the energy of the products
B. By raising the equilibrium concentration of products
C. By offering a lower-activation-energy pathway
D. By increasing the temperature without energy input [1]

(9) What are protein catalysts called?
A. Electrolytes
B. Enzymes
C. Indicators
D. Isotopes [1]

(10) Why can adding water restore blue colour to white anhydrous copper(II) sulfate?
A. Copper metal dissolves without oxidising
B. A different blue oxide forms
C. Sulfate changes to another anion
D. The blue hydrated salt reforms [1]

(11) A(aq) + B(aq) ⇌ C(aq) is at equilibrium. What response follows removal of some C at fixed temperature?
A. No shift; equilibrium remains unchanged
B. Forward shift; more C forms
C. Both forward and reverse reactions stop
D. Reverse shift; more A and B form [1]

(12) Which is the electron-transfer definition of oxidation?
A. Proton gain
B. Electron loss
C. Electron gain
D. Neutron loss [1]
items.canonical_answer:
(1) C. A new substance forms. New substance formation defines chemical change.
Distractor explanations: A: Shape can change without forming a new substance. B: Boiling can produce bubbles without chemical change. D: Heating alone can raise temperature without chemical change.

(2) A. It absorbs energy from surroundings. Energy enters the reacting system.
Distractor explanations: B: Releasing energy describes an exothermic reaction. C: Endothermic reactions have an energy change. D: Endothermic does not mean zero activation energy.

(3) A. 840 J. 50×4.2×4=840 J.
Distractor explanations: B: This results from dividing by the temperature change rather than multiplying. C: 0.84 is the value in kJ, not J. D: This omits the 4 °C temperature increase.

(4) C. Combustion transfers energy to the pan. Net reaction energy is transferred to the surroundings.
Distractor explanations: A: Breaking bonds requires energy; net release depends on forming product bonds. B: Energy is transferred from combustion to the pan, not absorbed by the fuel from it. D: The pan can warm by heat transfer without reacting chemically.

(5) A. No operating combustion; weather-dependent output. Moving air supplies energy without on-site fuel burning.
Distractor explanations: B: Wind output depends on wind speed and availability. C: Manufacture and construction still have environmental impacts. D: Wind generation transfers kinetic energy into electrical energy.

(6) D. A higher gas-production rate. Gradient is change in volume per unit time.
Distractor explanations: A: Gradient measures rate, not the final collected volume. B: A steeper rising curve means a faster, not slower, rate. C: Final volume is read at the plateau, not from steepness.

(7) D. Successful collisions occur more frequently. Concentration changes particle number per unit volume.
Distractor explanations: A: At constant temperature, average kinetic energy does not increase. B: Concentration does not lower the activation-energy barrier. C: Concentration changes encounter frequency, not the energy of each collision.

(8) C. By offering a lower-activation-energy pathway. More collisions can succeed along the lower-barrier pathway.
Distractor explanations: A: A catalyst changes the pathway, not product energy levels. B: It does not shift equilibrium composition. D: Catalysis does not create a temperature increase without energy transfer.

(9) B. Enzymes. Enzymes are biological protein catalysts.
Distractor explanations: A: Electrolytes conduct through mobile ions; this is not the name of protein catalysts. C: Indicators signal conditions such as pH, rather than naming protein catalysts. D: Isotopes are atoms of one element with different neutron counts.

(10) D. The blue hydrated salt reforms. Hydration reverses the intended dehydration change.
Distractor explanations: A: The starting substance is copper sulfate, not copper metal. B: The product is hydrated sulfate, not a new oxide. C: The sulfate ion remains sulfate; hydration changes water association.

(11) B. Forward shift; more C forms. The response tends to replace removed product.
Distractor explanations: A: Removing C disturbs equilibrium composition. C: Both reactions continue; neither simply stops. D: A reverse shift would remove more C rather than replace some of it.

(12) B. Electron loss. Oxidation is electron loss.
Distractor explanations: A: Proton transfer defines acid–base behaviour, not oxidation. C: Electron gain is reduction. D: Neutron loss is a nuclear process, not this redox definition.

items.prompt:
(a) Define reaction rate. [1]

(b) Describe two shared features of the Curve A and Curve B in visuals/VIS-6117-6-02.svg. Measurements: time / s: 0, 20, 40, 60, 80, 100, 120. Curve A CO2 volume / cm³: 0, 18, 30, 38, 43, 46, 48. Curve B CO2 volume / cm³: 0, 28, 41, 47, 48, 48, 48. Equal limiting masses of the same carbonate react with excess acid under matched temperature and acid conditions. Subsequent observations confirm both remain at 48 cm³. [2]

(c) Explain why a powder can react faster than an equal mass of chips of the same carbonate with excess acid under the same conditions. [2]

(d) Compare the initial gas-production rates of the Curve B and Curve A using the first 20 s of the supplied observations. Measurements: time / s: 0, 20, 40, 60, 80, 100, 120. Curve A CO2 volume / cm³: 0, 18, 30, 38, 43, 46, 48. Curve B CO2 volume / cm³: 0, 28, 41, 47, 48, 48, 48. Equal limiting masses of the same carbonate react with excess acid under matched temperature and acid conditions. Subsequent observations confirm both remain at 48 cm³. [1]

![Question stimulus](visuals/VIS-6117-6-02.svg)
items.canonical_answer:
(a) Change in reactant or product quantity per unit time.

(b) Both rise rapidly initially and then flatten as rate falls; both reach the same final 48 cm³.

(c) Powder has a larger exposed surface area, allowing more frequent successful collisions between acid particles and the solid surface.

(d) Curve B is initially faster: it gives 28 cm³ in 20 s compared with 18 cm³ for chips.
marking_guidance: Part a: Quantity change per unit time (1).
Part b: Initially steeper then flattening (1).
Part b: Same final 48 cm³ (1).
Part c: Larger exposed area (1).
Part c: More frequent successful surface collisions (1).
Part d: Powder faster, consistent with first-interval data (1).

items.prompt:
(a) Plot chip CO2 volume against time on the blank grid visuals/VIS-6117-6-blank.svg or suitable graph paper, with labelled axes and a smooth curve. Measurements: time / s: 0, 20, 40, 60, 80, 100, 120. Chip CO2 volume / cm³: 0, 18, 30, 38, 43, 46, 48. Powder CO2 volume / cm³: 0, 28, 41, 47, 48, 48, 48. Equal limiting masses of the same carbonate react with excess acid under matched temperature and acid conditions. Subsequent observations confirm both remain at 48 cm³. [3]

(b) Calculate the average chip gas-production rate from 20 s to 60 s. The collected CO2 volume is 18 cm³ at 20 s and 38 cm³ at 60 s. [2]

(c) State a suitable apparatus for measuring the volume of gas produced by carbonate reacting with excess acid. [1]

(d) Plan a teacher-supervised investigation of how dilute hydrochloric acid concentration affects the initial rate of CO2 production from carbonate chips. Include the changed variable, controls, measurements and a comparison supporting a conclusion. [6]

![Question stimulus](visuals/VIS-6117-6-blank.svg)
items.canonical_answer:
(a) Plot (0,0), (20,18), (40,30), (60,38), (80,43), (100,46), (120,48), with time / s horizontal and CO2 volume / cm³ vertical. Draw a smooth rising curve with decreasing gradient, without overshooting 48 cm³. The answer panel is visuals/VIS-6117-6-chip-answer.svg.

(b) Average rate=(38−18)/(60−20)=20/40=0.50 cm³/s.

(c) A gas syringe with a freely moving plunger.

(d) Connect a carbonate reaction flask by a bung and unobstructed delivery tube to a freely moving gas syringe. Vary dilute hydrochloric acid concentration over several stated values, keeping acid volume fixed and acid in excess in every trial. Keep carbonate mass and particle-size range fixed and maintain the same starting temperature. Start the clock consistently on mixing and record gas volume at the same short time intervals. Repeat each concentration and compare mean initial gradients or mean gas volume per equal early interval, with units, to conclude how concentration affects rate. Check for leaks and timing delay; wear eye protection under teacher supervision.
marking_guidance: Part a: Suitable axes and units (1).
Part a: All points within ±1 cm³ at correct times (1).
Part a: Smooth sensible curve with decreasing gradient, no overshoot (1).
Part b: Volume change divided by time change (1).
Part b: 0.50 cm³/s (1); accept 0.48–0.52 from allowed graphical readings and correct follow-through.
Part c: Gas syringe (1); accept a suitable graduated water-displacement arrangement.
Part d: Workable gas-collection method (1).
Part d: Vary acid concentration explicitly (1).
Part d: Control carbonate mass and size (1).
Part d: Control temperature (1).
Part d: Gas volumes at fixed timed intervals (1).
Part d: Compare initial rates to form conclusion (1). Accept an equivalent safe mass-loss method with timed measurements and appropriate controls; maximum six marks.
